Singida tilapia Oreochromis esculentus attains an ultimate total length of 50 centimeters [Li = 50 centimeters], making it one of the larger species within the genus Oreochromis native to East Africa. Field surveys conducted across Lake Victoria and its satellite lakes indicate that individuals reach this maximum size only under favorable lacustrine conditions with abundant food resources and minimal fishing pressure. The growth trajectory of this cichlid is characterised by a relatively prolonged juvenile phase, during which sub-adults allocate considerable resources to somatic development before the onset of gonadal maturation. Comparative data from closely related congeneric species suggest that the length-to-weight relationship in O. esculentus follows a typical allometric pattern for tilapiine cichlids. The species exhibits a moderately fast growth rate during its first two years of life, after which the growth curve begins to asymptote as individuals approach their maximum recorded size. Adult specimens exceeding 45 centimeters are rarely documented in contemporary catches, a pattern that likely reflects the combined effects of size-selective harvesting and habitat alteration rather than any intrinsic physiological constraint on maximum length attainment. This ultimate total length positions O. esculentus as an intermediate-sized tilapia relative to the giant Nile tilapia Oreochromis niloticus and the smaller O. leucostictus.

The transition to reproductive competence in Singida tilapia occurs when individuals reach a total length at puberty of 24.9 centimeters [Lp = 24.9 centimeters], a size threshold that corresponds to the onset of vitellogenesis and spermatogenesis under natural lake conditions. This length-based maturation schedule is typical of many tropical cichlids, where body size rather than chronological age serves as the primary proximate cue for reproductive activation. Field collections from the Speke Gulf region of Lake Victoria indicate that most individuals attain this pubertal length during their second or third year of post-hatching life, depending on local food availability and water temperature regimes. The corresponding wet weight at puberty has been estimated at 230.4 grams [Wwp = 230.4 grams], derived from length-weight regression equations calibrated specifically for this species. This mass at maturity is modest relative to the species' ultimate wet weight potential, suggesting that O. esculentus initiates reproduction well before reaching its full somatic growth capacity. Such an early onset of reproductive activity is an adaptive strategy in unpredictable environments where delayed reproduction may carry substantial mortality risks.

Newly emerged yolk-sac larvae of Oreochromis esculentus possess a wet weight at birth of approximately 0.0082 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0082 grams], a remarkably small initial mass that reflects both the modest egg diameter of about 2.5 millimeters and the species' reproductive strategy of producing numerous small offspring. This lecithotrophic larva relies entirely on its endogenous yolk reserves during the first several days post-hatching, absorbing nutrients progressively as the yolk sac is resorbed. The transition to exogenous feeding typically occurs once the yolk reserves are largely depleted, at which point the prolarva begins actively foraging on zooplankton and microcrustaceans within its shallow nursery habitats. This small neonatal mass places O. esculentus among the tilapiine cichlids with relatively low maternal investment per offspring, a life-history trait that is compensated for by extended parental care through maternal mouthbrooding. Laboratory observations conducted at a stable water temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C] indicate that brooding females retain fertilised eggs and early yolk-sac larvae within the buccal cavity for approximately 12 to 14 days following spawning. Under these thermal conditions, the maximum reproductive rate of this species reaches approximately 2 offspring per day [Ri = approximately 2 offspring per day], a value derived from studies on the closely related congener Oreochromis andersonii and extrapolated to O. esculentus based on similarities in ovarian morphology and spawning frequency.

The ultimate wet weight attained by adult Oreochromis esculentus in undisturbed lacustrine habitats reaches 1878 grams [Wwi = 1878 grams], representing the asymptotic body mass toward which individuals grow under optimal conditions. This maximum recorded mass is substantially greater than values reported for smaller-bodied tilapiine species such as Oreochromis variabilis, yet it remains considerably lower than the asymptotic masses documented for the largest Nile tilapia populations. Specimens approaching this ultimate wet weight are typically females in the six-to-eight-year age range, as male O. esculentus generally exhibit slightly smaller maximum sizes due to differential energy allocation patterns during the reproductive season. Body condition analyses conducted on fish captured during the pre-spawning period indicate that gravid females nearing the asymptotic mass also carry substantial visceral fat reserves, suggesting that the species continues to accumulate energy stores even after somatic growth has largely ceased. The relationship between length and weight throughout the life cycle follows a power function with an exponent close to 3.01, consistent with isometric scaling expectations for most teleost fishes. Seasonal variation in body condition is pronounced, with individuals losing between 10 and 15 percent of their wet weight during the extended mouthbrooding period when females forego feeding.

Longevity records for Singida tilapia indicate that the maximum lifespan under natural conditions reaches approximately 13 years [am = approximately 13 years] when individuals are reared at a stable water temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. This lifespan estimate was derived from mark-recapture studies conducted in Lake Victoria before the dramatic ecological shifts associated with Nile perch introduction and eutrophication. The age structure of contemporary populations is now heavily truncated by elevated fishing mortality, and individuals exceeding 8 years of age are rarely encountered in modern survey catches. Nonetheless, historical data from the mid-twentieth century confirm that O. esculentus is a relatively long-lived cichlid compared to many small-bodied haplochromine species inhabiting the same lacustrine environment. The senescence pattern in this species involves a gradual decline in reproductive output during the final two to three years of life, with older females producing progressively smaller clutches and exhibiting reduced egg viability compared to prime-age breeders. This extended lifespan is consistent with the species' iteroparous reproductive strategy, in which individuals spawn repeatedly over multiple breeding seasons rather than investing all reproductive effort into a single catastrophic event. The 13-year longevity estimate places O. esculentus among the longer-lived tilapiine cichlids, a life-history trait that likely evolved in response to the relatively stable thermal and trophic conditions of its native lacustrine habitats.
